content: Magnesium sulphate is a widely used treatment in perinatal care. Its role in reducing the risk of cerebral palsy in children when administered to women at risk of preterm birth was established in a 2009 Cochrane review. Since then, additional randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and extended follow-up studies have been conducted, leading to an updated review of its effectiveness and safety. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of magnesium sulphate as a neuroprotective agent for fetuses when given to women at risk of preterm birth. The review included RCTs and cluster-RCTs that compared magnesium sulphate with placebo or no treatment in women at risk of preterm birth before 34 weeks of gestation. Studies focusing on magnesium sulphate for tocolysis or for the prevention/treatment of eclampsia were excluded. Data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) and mean differences, with the certainty of evidence assessed using the GRADE approach. Six RCTs involving 5917 women and 6759 fetuses were included, all conducted in high-income countries. The studies demonstrated that magnesium sulphate, compared to placebo, reduced the risk of cerebral palsy in children up to two years of corrected age (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.89) and the combined outcome of death or cerebral palsy (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.98). The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one case of cerebral palsy was 60, and for death or cerebral palsy, it was 56. These findings were supported by high-certainty evidence. Magnesium sulphate likely had little to no effect on the risk of death (fetal, neonatal, or later) (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.13), major neurodevelopmental disability (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.44), or the combined outcome of death or major neurodevelopmental disability (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.07). These outcomes were supported by moderate-certainty evidence. At early school age, magnesium sulphate may have had little to no effect on death (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.02), cerebral palsy (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.41), the combined outcome of death or cerebral palsy (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.20), or the combined outcome of death or major neurodevelopmental disability (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.12). These findings were based on low-certainty evidence. The effect of magnesium sulphate on major neurodevelopmental disability was very uncertain (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.62; very low-certainty evidence). Magnesium sulphate probably reduced the risk of severe intraventricular hemorrhage (grade 3 or 4) in infants (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.98), with an NNT of 92. However, it may have had little to no effect on the risk of chronic lung disease or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.10). The evidence for these outcomes was of moderate and low certainty, respectively. For maternal outcomes, magnesium sulphate may have had little to no effect on severe maternal complications such as death, cardiac arrest, or respiratory arrest (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.92; low-certainty evidence). However, it probably increased the likelihood of maternal adverse effects severe enough to require discontinuation of treatment (RR 3.21, 95% CI 1.88 to 5.48; moderate-certainty evidence). Magnesium sulphate likely had little to no effect on the rates of cesarean section (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.02) or postpartum hemorrhage (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.09), based on moderate-certainty evidence. Data on breastfeeding at hospital discharge and women’s perspectives on treatment were not reported. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that magnesium sulphate reduces the risk of cerebral palsy and the combined outcome of death or cerebral palsy in children up to two years of corrected age. It also likely reduces the risk of severe intraventricular hemorrhage in infants. However, it may have little to no effect on other outcomes, such as death or major neurodevelopmental disability, particularly at school age. For mothers, while severe complications are unlikely, magnesium sulphate probably increases the risk of adverse effects significant enough to discontinue treatment. Further research is needed to explore the long-term benefits and risks for children into adolescence and adulthood, as well as to assess the generalizability of findings to lowand middle-income countries.
